## Overview

In this module we demonstrate some basic transformations on DataFrames:
* Working with columns
    * Selecting columns
    * Dropping columns
    * Specifying columns
    * Adding columns
    * Changing the column name
    * Changing the column type
* Working with rows
    * Ordering rows
    * Keeping a fixed number of rows
    * Keeping distinct rows
    * Filtering rows
    * Sampling rows
    * Working with missing values

**Note:** There is often more than one way to do these transformations.

%md
# Setup
---

%pyspark

# Read the raw data from HDFS:

rides = spark.read.csv("/duocar/raw/rides/", header=True, inferSchema=True)
rides.printSchema()

drivers = spark.read.csv("/duocar/raw/drivers/", header=True, inferSchema=True)
drivers.printSchema()

riders = spark.read.csv("/duocar/raw/riders/", header=True, inferSchema=True)
riders.printSchema()

%md
# Lesson
---

%md
## Spark SQL DataFrames

* Spark SQL DataFrames are inspired by R data frames and Python pandas DataFrames


* Spark SQL DataFrames are resilient distributed structured tables
    * A DataFrame is a distributed collection of *Row* objects
    * A Row object is an ordered collection of objects with names and types


* Properties of DataFrames
    * Immutable - DataFrames are read-only
    * Evaluated lazily - Spark only does work when it has to
    * Ephemeral - DataFrames disappear unless explicitly persisted

* Operations on DataFrames
    * *Transformations* return a DataFrame
        * Narrow Transformations
        * Wide Transformations
    * *Actions* cause Spark to do work

* Spark SQL provides two APIs
    * SQL
    * DataFrame

* Spark SQL code is declarative - the Catalyst optimizer produces core Spark RDD code

%md
## Working with Columns

paragraphs.title: Selecting Columns
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `select` method to select specific columns:
riders.select("birth_date", "student", "sex").printSchema()

paragraphs.title: Dropping Columns
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `drop` method to drop specific columns:
riders.drop("first_name", "last_name", "ethnicity").printSchema()

paragraphs.title: Specifying Columns
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# We have used the column name to reference a DataFrame column:
riders.select("first_name").printSchema()

# We actually work with `Column` objects in Spark SQL.
# Use the following syntax to reference a column object in a particular DataFrame:
riders.select(riders.first_name).printSchema()
riders.select(riders["first_name"]).printSchema()
type(riders["first_name"])

# Use the `col` function to reference a general column object:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col
riders.select(col("first_name")).printSchema()
type(col("first_name"))

# Use `*` (in quotes) to specify all columns:
riders.select("*").printSchema()

paragraphs.title: Adding Columns
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `withColumn` method to add a new column:
riders \
  .select("student") \
  .withColumn("student_boolean", col("student") == 1) \
  .show()

# The `select` method also works:
riders.select("student", (col("student") == 1).alias("student_boolean")).show(5)

# The `selectExpr` method accepts partial SQL expressions:
riders.selectExpr("student", "student = 1 as student_boolean").show(5)

# The `sql` method accepts full SQL statements:
riders.createOrReplaceTempView("riders_view")
spark.sql("select student, student = 1 as student_boolean from riders_view").show(5)

paragraphs.title: Changing the column name
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `withColumnRenamed` method to rename a column:
riders.withColumnRenamed("start_date", "join_date").printSchema()

# Chain multiple methods to rename more than one column:
riders \
  .withColumnRenamed("start_date", "join_date") \
  .withColumnRenamed("sex", "gender") \
  .printSchema()

paragraphs.title: Changing the column type
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Recall that `home_block` was read in as a (long) integer:
riders.printSchema()

# Use the `withColumn` (DataFrame) method in conjunction with the `cast`
# (Column) method to change its type:
riders.withColumn("home_block", col("home_block").cast("string")).printSchema()

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
If we need to change the name and/or type of many columns, then we may want to consider specifying the schema on read.

%md
## Working with rows

paragraphs.title: Ordering rows
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `sort` or `orderBy` method to sort a DataFrame by particular columns:
rides \
  .select("rider_id", "date_time") \
  .sort("rider_id", "date_time", ascending=True) \
  .show()

rides \
  .select("rider_id", "date_time") \
  .orderBy("rider_id", "date_time", ascending=False) \
  .show()

# Use the `asc` and `desc` methods to specify the sort order:
rides \
  .select("rider_id", "date_time") \
  .sort(col("rider_id").asc(), col("date_time").desc()) \
  .show()

# Alternatively, use the `asc` and `desc` functions to specify the sort order:
from pyspark.sql.functions import asc, desc
rides \
  .select("rider_id", "date_time") \
  .orderBy(asc("rider_id"), desc("date_time")) \
  .show()

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
Ascending order is the default.

paragraphs.title: Selecting a fixed number of rows
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `limit` method to select a fixed number of rows:
riders.select("student", "sex").limit(5).show()

paragraphs.title: Question
paragraphs.text:
%md
What is the difference between `df.show(5)` and `df.limit(5).show()`?

1. df.show(5)
What it does: It directly triggers an action that takes the top 5 records from the partitions and renders them in an ASCII table on the driver's console/output.
Return type: Unit (Scala) or None (Python).
Use case: Quick ad-hoc data inspection when you just want to take a peak at the dataframe without modifying or storing it.

2. df.limit(5).show()
What it does:
df.limit(5) is a lazy transformation that builds a new DataFrame restricted to at most 5 rows. It adds a Limit logical operator to Spark's Execution Plan.
.show() is the action chained at the end, which evaluates that new limited DataFrame and prints all of its rows (since default .show() prints 20 rows, and this DataFrame only contains 5).
Return type for df.limit(5): A new DataFrame / Dataset[Row].

paragraphs.title: Selecting distinct rows
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `distinct` method to select distinct rows:
riders.select("student", "sex").distinct().show()

# You can also use the `dropDuplicates` method:
riders.select("student", "sex").dropDuplicates().show()

paragraphs.title: Filtering rows
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `filter` or `where` method along with a Boolean column expression to select particular rows:
riders.filter(col("student") == 1).count()
riders.where(col("sex") == "female").count()
riders.filter(col("student") == 1).where(col("sex") == "female").count()

paragraphs.title: Sampling rows
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `sample` method to select a random sample of rows with or without
# replacement:
riders.count()
riders.sample(withReplacement=False, fraction=0.1, seed=12345).count()

# Use the `sampleBy` method to select a stratified random sample:
riders \
  .groupBy("sex") \
  .count() \
  .show() 
riders \
  .sampleBy("sex", fractions={"male": 0.2, "female": 0.8}, seed=54321) \
  .groupBy("sex") \
  .count() \
  .show()

# We have randomly sampled 20% of the male riders and 80% of the female riders.

paragraphs.title: Working with missing values
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Note the missing (null) values in the following DataFrame:
riders_selected = riders.select("id", "sex", "ethnicity")
riders_selected.show(25)

# Drop rows with any missing values:
riders_selected.dropna(how="any", subset=["sex", "ethnicity"]).show(25)

# Drop rows with all missing values:
riders_selected.na.drop(how="all", subset=["sex", "ethnicity"]).show(25)

# Replace missing values with a common value:
riders_selected.fillna("OTHER/UNKNOWN", ["sex", "ethnicity"]).show(25)

# Replace missing values with different values:
riders_missing = riders_selected.na.fill({"sex": "OTHER/UNKNOWN", "ethnicity": "MISSING"})
riders_missing.show(25)

# Replace arbitrary values with a common value:
riders_missing.replace(["OTHER/UNKNOWN", "MISSING"], "NA", ["sex", "ethnicity"]).show(25)

# Replace arbitrary values with different values:
riders_missing.na.replace({"OTHER/UNKNOWN": "NA", "MISSING": "NO RESPONSE"}, None, ["sex", "ethnicity"]).show(25)

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md

* `dropna` and `na.drop` are equivalent.
* `fillna` and `na.fill` are equivalent.
* The fill value type must match the column type.
* `replace` and `na.replace` are equivalent.

%md
# Lab
---

paragraphs.title: 1 - Replace the missing values in `rides.service` with the string `Car`
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Select only the column "service" of dataframe "rides", deleting the duplication of the column "service" and then show rows in ASCII text table format.
rides.select("service").distinct().show()

# Create a new dataframe called "rides_filled" copying the original, but searching null values in the column "service" and replacing them with the string "Car"
rides_filled = rides.fillna("Car", subset=["service"])

# Select only the column "service" from the dataframe "rides_filled", deleting the duplication of the column "service" and then show rows in ASCII text table format.
rides_filled.select("service").distinct().show()

paragraphs.title: 2 - Rename `rides.cancelled` to `rides.canceled`
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Creaing a new dataframe called "rides_renamed" and renaming the column "cancelled" to "canceled" into it.
rides_renamed = rides.withColumnRenamed("cancelled", "canceled").printSchema()

paragraphs.title: 3 - Sort the `rides` DataFrame in descending order with respect to # `driver_id` and ascending order with respect to `date_time`
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Importing functioncs "asc" and "desc" from PySpark functions module.
from pyspark.sql.functions import asc, desc

# Assigning the transformation to a dataframe called "rides_sorted". The "\" specifies that the instruction continues to the next line.
# Selection only the columns "driver_id" and "date_time".
# Order the rows of the dataframe by applying a double standard: First, order by the column "date_time" in ascending order, then if 2 rows have the same value, it will break the tie by sorting the "driver_id" column in descending order.
# It will execute the spark action and it will show the first 20 rows.
rides_sorted = rides \
  .select("driver_id", "date_time") \
  .orderBy(asc("date_time"), desc("driver_id")) \
  .show()

paragraphs.title: 4 - Create an 20% random sample of the `rides` DataFrame
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# A spark action, count and return rows total number of the dataframe.
rides.count()

# This is a transformation that creates a new DataFrame called rides_sampled by taking a random sample from the original DataFrame. Its parameters mean the following:
# withReplacement=False: Sampling without replacement. This means that the same row cannot be selected more than once in the sample.
# fraction=0.2: Instructs Spark to extract approximately 20% of the data (one-fifth of the total dataset).
# seed=31416: The random seed. By setting a specific number (in this case, 31416), you ensure reproducibility: every time you run this cell, Spark will select the exact same random rows.
rides_sampled = rides.sample(withReplacement=False, fraction=0.2, seed=31416)

# In this action will count again the rows number of the new dataframe
rides_sampled.count()

paragraphs.title: 5 - Remove the driver's name from the `drivers` DataFrame
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Deleting the columns "first_name" and "last_name"
drivers_phantom = drivers.drop("first_name", "last_name").show()

paragraphs.title: 6 - How many drivers have signed up?
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# This action count the total number of drivers
drivers.count()

paragraphs.title: 7 - How many female drivers have signed up?
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# This action count the total number of female drivers by using the "filter" function to filter by sex in the column "sex"
drivers.filter(drivers.sex == "female").count()

paragraphs.title: 8 - How many non-white, female drivers have signed up?
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# This action count the total number of non-white female drivers by using the "filter" function to filter by ethnicity in the column "ethnicity" and by using the function "where" to filter by female drivers with the column "sex"
drivers.filter(col("ethnicity") != "White").where(col("sex") == "female").count()
